title: Xinference Llama3 tool-call parser eval()s model output (serving-layer RCE)
attacker_story: Xinference serves models over an OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions API (unauthenticated by default). When a request carries a tools field, the non-streaming Transformers path calls _post_process_completion, which hands the model's completion to the Llama3 tool-call parser. In 2.5.0 Llama3ToolParser.extract_tool_calls parses that completion with eval(model_output, {}, {}) -- so any Python expression the model emits runs on the server. A prompt-injected or adversarially-steered model that returns __import__('os').system(...) achieves remote code execution in the serving layer. No model is needed to prove it: the scripted model stands in for the completion the injection would elicit; the finding is that the framework eval()s model output with no guard (GHSA-x2rj-828p-hx9m, fixed in 2.7.0 by switching to json.loads / ast.literal_eval, commit 1b3d220f).

scripted_model.interface: the raw model completion string fed to Llama3ToolParser.extract_tool_calls (the framework's own tool-call parsing entry point for Transformers-backend chat results)
scripted_model.behavior: returns the attacker-chosen completion verbatim; the parser eval()s it. Proves the serving framework lacks a guard independent of which model produced the text.
scripted_model.may_assume: that some untrusted prompt could steer a real model into emitting this completion -- an in-shape Llama3 tool-call payload, i.e. a Python expression, which is exactly what this parser eval()s; nothing more
scripted_model.may_not_assume: no auth bypass beyond the documented default (auth off by default per the advisory), no network, no attacker-controlled config or secret; only that the model's text reaches the parser

canary.mechanism: the eval'd expression runs __import__('os').system('echo <nonce> > /tmp/chainlab_canary'); oracle reads the file and checks the per-trial nonce
